1387.title: Welcoming seekers
1387.hook: Sikhs welcome seekers without pressing anyone to convert
1387.howItsDone: Gurdwaras are open to visitors of any background, who are asked only to cover their heads, remove their shoes and refrain from tobacco and alcohol; the langar serves everyone, and taking amrit is a personal choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, other paths: Sheikh Farid in the Granth, and Guru Tegh Bahadur defending a freedom that wasn't his own. Your line was respect the sincere.

A first-time visitor stands at the gurdwara door, unsure. Shoes? Head? Is it all right to be here at all? Someone notices. A scarf is offered for covering the head. A hand points: over there, the langar, if you're hungry. Nobody asks what the visitor believes. Nobody hands over a sign-up sheet. The visitor eats, listens to the kirtan for a while, maybe asks a question, and leaves when they like. That ease isn't the accident of one friendly person. It runs through the way the Gurus dealt with seekers.
screen: `A STRANGER AT THE DOOR.` → `A SCARF, A PLATE.` → `NO SIGN-UP SHEET.`

segments.voice: First, a friend to all. A hymn of Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to everyone. The posture toward a stranger starts there, not with a sales pitch. Second, questions welcomed. We've sat with the Siddhas twice already; look at the Sidh Gosht once more, this time for its manner. The yogis test Guru Nanak with hard questions. He answers, verse by verse; they push back, and he answers again. Nobody is shamed for asking. A seeker's question is worth a careful answer. Third, no pressure. The Gurus' own stories favor invitation over insistence: Guru Nanak traveling, singing, talking with whoever came. Anyone may sit in the sangat, eat in the langar, hear the Granth read. Some who come later choose to take amrit and join the Khalsa. That choice is theirs, and it's meant to be free, or it means nothing. Fourth, the hard part. It's easy to welcome someone who agrees with you. It's harder to welcome the person whose question sounds like a challenge, or who leaves unpersuaded. The Gurus' way treats that person as a guest, fed and honored, not a project.
screen: `GURU ARJAN: A FRIEND TO EVERYONE.` · `SIDH GOSHT: HARD QUESTIONS ANSWERED.` · `NO CAMPAIGN, A FREE CHOICE.` · `A GUEST, NOT A PROJECT.` · then, large: `WELCOME, NOT PRESSURE.`

segments.voice: Recall a question someone once asked you about something you care about, your faith, your work, your family's ways, that made you bristle. Breathe in and hear it again without the bristle. Breathe out and imagine answering the way you'd pour tea for a guest: unhurried, warm, with no need for them to agree.
Welcoming seekers. Sikhs welcome anyone to the gurdwara and the langar, answer questions as Guru Nanak did in the Sidh Gosht, and leave the choice free. Today's word.
Your line: welcome, not pressure. A guest is free to leave still deciding. Until tomorrow.

1388.title: God in nature
1388.hook: Nanak says he is a sacrifice to the One who dwells in creation (Asa di Var, ang 469)
1388.howItsDone: Asa di Var is sung in gurdwaras in the early morning; Sikhs read its lines on kudrat as saying the Creator dwells in creation while remaining beyond it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, welcoming seekers: a stranger at the gurdwara door, and hard questions answered with care. Your line was welcome, not pressure.

Balihari. It's a word of love so strong it borrows the language of offering: I am a sacrifice to you, I'd give myself for you. In Punjabi homes it can be said over a child. In the Granth it's said to God. And in one line of Asa di Var, the hymn sung in the early morning, Guru Nanak says where he finds the One he'd give himself for. Not in a temple. Not up past the clouds. Right here, in the made world, in the stuff of a walk outside.
screen: `BALIHARI: I'D GIVE MYSELF FOR YOU.` → `ASA DI VAR, IN THE EARLY MORNING.` → `NOT PAST THE CLOUDS. RIGHT HERE.`

segments.voice: First, the line, at Ang four hundred sixty-nine. In paraphrase: I am a sacrifice to You, who dwell in Your creation; Your limit cannot be known. The word for creation is kudrat: nature, the made world, and also the power that makes it. The One isn't parked somewhere outside it, looking in. Second, what kudrat holds. Earlier in Asa di Var, in a salok, Guru Nanak runs through it. In paraphrase: by Your power we see, by Your power we hear; Yours are the earth and the skies, the air and the water and the fire, the creatures of every kind, even fear and comfort. It reads like someone standing outdoors, turning slowly, naming. Third, in, not equal to. The same line says the One's limit can't be known. The Creator dwells in creation and isn't used up by it. A field at dawn is not the whole of God, but nothing in it is empty of God either. Fourth, an ordinary walk. If the One dwells in the made world, then a pigeon on a wire, a weed in a sidewalk crack, rain running down a window are not background. They're places to look. And Guru Nanak's answer to seeing them isn't a theory. It's balihari: love so full it wants to give itself.

segments.voice: If you can, step outside or stand at a window, and let your eyes rest on one living thing: a tree, a patch of grass, a bird, a cloud moving. Don't name it or judge it; just look, the way Guru Nanak turns slowly and lists. If your mind drifts, come back to the one thing.
God in nature. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak offers himself to the One who dwells in kudrat, the made world, and whose limit cannot be known. Today's word.
Your line: he dwells in nature. Nothing in the made world is empty of the One. See you tomorrow.

1389.title: Caring for the earth
1389.hook: the earth is the great mother of the Japji's last salok
1389.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Japji each morning, ending with the salok that calls air the Guru, water the father and the earth the great mother; some Sikh groups plant trees and clean rivers in its spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kudrat: Guru Nanak giving himself to the One who dwells in creation. Your line was he dwells in nature.

Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end on its last salok, and it sounds less like the close of a hymn than a family introduction. Here is your teacher. Here is your father. Here is your mother. And the names that follow aren't people. They're air, and water, and the ground under your feet. After a long climb through the Japji's thought, it's a strange and lovely way to come down: back onto the earth, like a child into a lap.
screen: `THE JAPJI'S LAST SALOK.` → `A FAMILY INTRODUCTION.` → `AIR, WATER, EARTH.`

segments.voice: First, the family. You met this salok's sound early on this path, when the Japji closed: pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat. In paraphrase: air is the Guru, water is the father, and the earth is the great mother. A family, with roles. Air teaches, the way breath and sound carry the Word. Water gives life, the way a father is said to. The earth holds and feeds. Second, the lap. The salok goes on, in paraphrase: day and night are the two nurses, and the whole world plays in their lap. Light and dark take shifts, like two caregivers. Third, the reckoning. Then the tone changes. Good and bad deeds are read out before the Lord, and each person's own actions bring them near or send them far. The child playing in the lap is also answerable for how it plays. Fourth, what family does. You don't strip your mother's house. You don't foul your father's water. If the earth is the great mother, caring for it isn't a cause bolted onto faith; it's how you treat family. Some Sikhs have taken the salok as the heart of environmental work, planting trees and cleaning rivers in its name. The Japji ends on the ground, among relatives, with the day's account still open.
screen: `AIR THE GURU, WATER THE FATHER.` · `DAY AND NIGHT: TWO NURSES.` · `DEEDS READ OUT.` · `YOU DON'T STRIP YOUR MOTHER'S HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE GREAT MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Feel the air going in: the Guru, the salok says. Feel your weight on the floor or the ground beneath you: the great mother, holding you up without being asked. Stay with that for a few breaths, and let one small piece of earth you could care for come to mind: a plant, a patch of ground, a tap left running.
Caring for the earth. The Japji's last salok calls air the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother; caring for her is how family treats family. Today's word.
Your line: the great mother. Family looks after family, and the earth is family. Same time tomorrow.

1390.title: Wonder and discovery
1390.hook: the Granth's wonder at countless worlds sits easily with curiosity
1390.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of vismaad as the awe the Gurus describe before creation; the Japji's verse on worlds below and skies above is part of the daily morning prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Japji's last salok: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. Your line was the great mother.

Worlds below worlds. Skies above skies. That's how one verse of the Japji opens, and it keeps going: people have searched to the very edge and grown tired, and the edge still isn't found. If the count could be written down, it would be, but the writing runs out first. And the Granth's response to a creation too big to measure isn't fear, or a closed door. It's a word the Gurus come back to with delight.
screen: `WORLDS BELOW WORLDS. SKIES ABOVE SKIES.` → `THE WRITING RUNS OUT FIRST.` → `NOT FEAR. DELIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Vismaad: wonder, awe, the astonished stillness when something is bigger than your mind can hold. It isn't confusion. It's being overwhelmed in the right direction. Second, the Japji's map. Guru Nanak describes creation as layered past counting, and says plainly it can't be fully written down. That's not a ban on looking. It's an honest note about scale: however far you go, there's farther. Third, the wonder hymn, which you met early on this path. In Asa di Var the word rings again and again. In paraphrase: wonder the sound, wonder the Vedas, the books of knowledge; wonder the creatures, wonder their kinds; wonder the forms, wonder the colors; wonder the wind, the water, the fire at play; wonder the near, wonder the far. Look at what sits in that list. The books of knowledge stand right beside the wind and the fire. Learning isn't the end of wonder there. It's one of the wonders. Fourth, curiosity. Some fear that learning how the world works drains the awe out of it. The Granth's picture runs the other way: the more you see, the more there is to be astonished by. A Sikh astronomer, or a child with a microscope, isn't trespassing on the sacred. They're doing vismaad with better instruments. Discovery doesn't close the book. It turns a page and finds the book is bigger than you thought.
screen: `VISMAAD: AWE PAST WHAT THE MIND HOLDS.` · `JAPJI: WORLDS PAST COUNTING.` · `ASA DI VAR: EVEN KNOWLEDGE IS A WONDER.` · `DISCOVERY TURNS THE PAGE.` · then, large: `WONDER KEEPS LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing about the night sky that's hard to picture: how far, how many, how old. Hold it gently, and on the in-breath let it be large; on the out-breath, notice whether the bigness feels like a threat or a gift. If you can, let the word come quietly with the out-breath: vismaad.
Vismaad. Wonder, awe, the astonished stillness before a creation too big to hold; in Asa di Var, even the books of knowledge are among the wonders. Today's word.
Your line: wonder keeps learning, not wonder stops learning. Every new fact is one more wonder. Until tomorrow.

1391.title: The ages
1391.hook: the Granth uses the four ages as a poetic frame for moral decline and renewal
1391.howItsDone: Sikhs read the Granth's ages, Satjug to Kaljug, as a poetic frame for the state of the heart, and hold that the Name and singing God's praise carry a person through the dark age.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vismaad: worlds below worlds, and wonder that grows as you learn. Your line was wonder keeps learning.

Things were better once. People say it about manners, music, neighbors, prices. The old Indian world gave that feeling a grand shape: the ages, each darker than the one before, sliding toward the last and hardest, the Kaljug. The Gurus inherited that frame. They didn't throw it away. But in their hands it stops being a calendar to calculate and becomes something closer to a mirror.
screen: `THINGS WERE BETTER ONCE.` → `THE AGES, DARKER AND DARKER.` → `NOT A CALENDAR. A MIRROR.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Jug, or yuga, means an age. The Granth names them: Satjug, Treta, Duapar, and Kaljug, the dark age, the one the hymns place us in. Second, the chariots. In a salok in Asa di Var, Guru Nanak gives each age a chariot and a driver. In paraphrase: in Satjug, contentment was the chariot and righteousness the charioteer; in Treta, restraint the chariot and strength the charioteer; in Duapar, austerity the chariot and truth the charioteer; in Kaljug, the fire of craving is the chariot and falsehood holds the reins. Notice what changes. Not the scenery. The virtues. Each age is described by what drives people. Third, the mirror. So it reads as poetry about the heart, not a timetable. The Kaljug isn't only out there in history. It's wherever craving is the vehicle and a lie is steering, and Satjug is wherever contentment carries a life and righteousness guides it. A single day can pass through more than one age. Fourth, renewal. The Granth doesn't leave the dark age hopeless. The Japji's very first salok says the True One was true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and will be true. The ages turn; the True One doesn't. And the hymns point to the Name, and to singing the praise, as what carries a person through a dark age. Decline is real. So is the way back.
screen: `JUG: AN AGE.` · `A CHARIOT AND A DRIVER FOR EACH AGE.` · `THE AGES AS A MIRROR OF THE HEART.` · `TRUE THROUGH THE AGES.` · then, large: `AGES TURN.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last day or so for a moment when craving was the chariot and something false held the reins: a rush, a grab, a small lie to get by. Just notice it, without scolding. Then find a moment when contentment carried you and something true was steering, a meal enjoyed, an honest word, and breathe with that one.
Jug. An age; the Granth uses the ages, from Satjug to Kaljug, as a poetic frame for decline and renewal, with a chariot and a driver for each. Today's word.
Your line: ages turn. Both ages can pass through a single life, even a single day. Rest well.

1392.title: Why suffering
1392.hook: the Gurus call pain a medicine and never pretend it isn't pain
1392.howItsDone: Sikhs often meet hardship by turning to the Guru's word, saying Ardas with family and sangat, and serving others; Guru Nanak's line calling pain the medicine is often recalled in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jug: the ages as a mirror for decline and renewal. Your line was ages turn.

A man has been carrying something heavy for a long time, and he's sure the weight is his alone. Everyone else seems fine. Their doors look calm, their windows bright. So he climbs up high, high enough to see the whole town at once. And from up there he sees it. Smoke from this house. Smoke from that one. House after house, a fire burning inside. That climb is a couplet of Sheikh Farid, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. Today: why suffering.
screen: `ONE MAN, ONE WEIGHT, ONE CLIMB.` → `SMOKE FROM EVERY HOUSE.` → `WHY SUFFERING.`

segments.voice: First, Farid up high. In paraphrase: Farid, I thought the pain was mine alone, but pain is spread through the whole world; when I climbed up and looked, I saw this same fire in house after house. The couplet doesn't say the fire is small, or fake, or deserved. It says it's everywhere. The starting point is honesty. Second, a line from Guru Nanak in Asa di Var that sounds upside down: dukh daaroo, sukh rog bhaiaa. Pain became the medicine, and comfort became the disease. Why? The line goes on, in paraphrase: when there is comfort, the Lord is not remembered. Comfort lulls. Pain wakes. A hard week can ask what matters in an afternoon. Third, a medicine is still bitter. The Guru doesn't say it doesn't hurt. Nobody hands someone a bitter cup and calls it delicious. The Gurus' hymns hold real grief and real crying out; we heard one of those protests last week. Fourth, the medicine is for your own pain, not a verdict on someone else's. A Sikh can say of their own hard season, this woke me up. That's very different from telling a grieving neighbor their loss is good for them. Sikh life answers other people's pain the plain way: with food, with seva, with showing up. So the Gurus give no tidy answer to why. They give a way to stand in it: name the fire honestly, let it wake you, and don't leave anyone else alone with theirs.
screen: `FARID: A FIRE IN EVERY HOUSE.` · `PAIN THE MEDICINE, COMFORT THE DISEASE.` · `A MEDICINE IS STILL BITTER.` · `YOUR PAIN, NOT A VERDICT ON THEIRS.` · then, large: `DUKH DAAROO.`

segments.voice: Let one real pain come to mind, not the biggest, one you can hold for two minutes, and name it plainly in a few words, the way Farid named his fire, without arguing or telling it it's fine. Then gently ask whether it's waking anything up in you; if nothing comes, that's all right too. If you pray, you can hold it before God without dressing it up. If a pain feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Why suffering. The Gurus call pain a medicine, because it wakes us when comfort lulls us, and they never pretend it isn't pain. Today's word.
Your line: pain, honestly. Nobody has to stand alone with their fire. See you tomorrow.

1393.title: Death without fear
1393.hook: death is part of the order; the one who remembers is not afraid
1393.howItsDone: At a Sikh death, family and sangat gather for kirtan and Ardas, the evening prayer Kirtan Sohila is recited, and a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is often held; Sikh teaching discourages loud lamenting while honoring grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why suffering: pain as a bitter medicine, never pretended away. Your line was pain, honestly.

Clean sheets on the guest bed. A towel folded at the foot of it. Everyone in the house knows two things about the guest: they're welcome, and they're leaving. Nobody is shocked when the bag gets packed. That's simply what a guest does. The Guru Granth Sahib reaches for pictures like this: the world as a place we stay for a while, and leaving as part of the visit. It isn't easy dinner talk, and the Gurus speak about it calmly anyway. Death without fear.
screen: `A GUEST ROOM, MADE UP.` → `WELCOME, AND LEAVING.` → `DEATH WITHOUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: First, the order. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak says it in a few plain words. In paraphrase: whoever has come will go; each one's turn comes. Not a threat. A description. Death is inside the Hukam, the order of things, the way sunset is inside the day. Second, a surprising request. In a hymn in Raag Vadahans, sung at the time of mourning, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: don't call death bad, people, if you know how to truly die. He isn't saying grief is wrong; the same hymns are full of tears. He's saying death itself isn't the enemy. The question is how a life has been lived, and whether it was lived remembering. Third, Kabir, in a couplet you met early on this path. In paraphrase: the death the whole world fears fills my mind with joy, because in dying one meets the One who is perfect bliss. Some readers hear two deaths there: the death of the body, and the daily dying of the swollen self. Fourth, the fearless one. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, names the One as nirbhau, without fear. The Gurus teach that a person who keeps remembering the fearless One begins to share in that fearlessness. Fear may still come. It just stops being the thing remembered. The sheets were clean for a guest who was always going to leave, and that never made the welcome less.
screen: `WHOEVER HAS COME WILL GO.` · `DON'T CALL DEATH BAD.` · `KABIR: THE DEATH THE WORLD FEARS.` · `NIRBHAU: REMEMBER THE FEARLESS ONE.` · then, large: `UNAFRAID.`

segments.voice: Go gently; if this subject is raw for you right now, simply breathe and rest instead. Let the thought come quietly, this life is a visit: on the in-breath, notice you are here, alive, welcome; on the out-breath, let the leaving be part of it, without forcing anything. If you pray, you can hold the word nirbhau, without fear, in the breath. If grief or dark thoughts feel too heavy to carry alone, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Death without fear. Death is part of the Lord's order, and the Gurus teach that the one who remembers the fearless One need not be ruled by fear of it. Today's word.
Your line: unafraid. Welcome while the visit lasts, and calm when the bag is packed. I'll be here tomorrow.
